gloss: To spoil the appearance or the good name of something.
examples: One bad review will not *blemish* a solid reputation.
The scandal *blemished* a career that had been spotless for thirty years.
Her credit history is *blemished* by a single late payment.

gloss: To spoil or damage something badly over a long period.
examples: Empty storefronts *blight* the whole downtown.
A fungus *blighted* the potato crop two years running.
The town has been *blighted* by the closing of the mill.

gloss: To cover someone's eyes with a cloth so that they cannot see.
examples: They *blindfold* the contestants before the taste test.
The kidnappers *blindfolded* him and pushed him into a van.
She sat *blindfolded* while we hid the presents.

gloss: To hit or shock someone from a direction they were not watching.
examples: A question like that can *blindside* even an experienced speaker.
The layoffs *blindsided* the entire department.
I was completely *blindsided* by his resignation.

ru: покрываться волдырями, покрыться волдырями; натирать мозоли
transitivity: both — transitive (*new boots blistered my heels*), intransitive (*the paint blistered in the sun*)
gloss: To form, or to cause, small bubbles of fluid or air on a surface.
examples: Cheap shoes always *blister* my heels.
The paint *blistered* where the afternoon sun hit it.
His palms were *blistering* by the end of the first hour.

transitivity: both — transitive (*salt bloats you*), intransitive (*the budget bloated*)
gloss: To swell up, or to make something swell up, with liquid, gas or extra content.
examples: Too much salt will *bloat* you for days.
The payroll *bloated* to twice its original size.
The app has become *bloated* with features nobody asked for.

ru: избивать дубинкой, забить; принуждать грубым напором
gloss: To strike someone repeatedly with a heavy object, or to force them by crude pressure.
examples: Do not *bludgeon* your readers with statistics.
The victim had been *bludgeoned* with a length of pipe.
He kept *bludgeoning* us with the same argument all evening.

ru: допускать грубую ошибку, оплошать; брести наугад
gloss: To make a careless, serious mistake, or to move clumsily without looking.
examples: Even seasoned negotiators sometimes *blunder*.
He *blundered* into the meeting a full hour late.
The agency has *blundered* badly on this one.

gloss: To make something less sharp, less strong or less effective.
examples: Tax credits should *blunt* the impact of higher fuel prices.
Years of bad news *blunted* their outrage.
The medication has *blunted* the pain without removing it.

gloss: To talk in a loud, boastful or threatening way that has little behind it.
examples: Some candidates *bluster* when they have nothing to offer.
He *blustered* about suing everyone involved, then did nothing.
The wind was *blustering* against the windows all night.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the hotel boasts two pools*), intransitive (*he boasted all evening*)
gloss: To speak with too much pride about yourself, or to possess something impressive.
examples: The city *boasts* the largest public library in the state.
He *boasted* that he had never failed an exam.
She accepted the prize without *boasting* about it.

transitivity: both — intransitive (*the buoy bobbed*), transitive (*she bobbed her head*)
gloss: To move up and down with short, quick movements.
examples: Empty bottles *bob* along the edge of the harbor.
The apple *bobbed* back up to the surface.
Her head was *bobbing* in time with the music.
contrast: The b doubles before an ending: *bob → bobbed, bobbing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the silence boded trouble*), intransitive (*it bodes well*)
gloss: To be a sign of what is going to happen.
examples: Early sales figures *bode* well for the holiday season.
The long silence *boded* nothing good.
Two straight quarters of losses do not *bode* well for the company.
contrast: Almost always used with *well* or *ill*: *this bodes well for us*.

ru: поражать, ошеломлять; не укладываться в голове
transitivity: both — transitive (*it boggles the mind*), intransitive (*the mind boggles*)
gloss: To overwhelm someone's mind so that it cannot take something in.
examples: The size of the national debt *boggles* the mind.
The numbers *boggled* everyone at the table.
It is still *boggling* my mind that she said yes.

ru: незаконно производить или продавать; торговать контрабандой
gloss: To make, copy or sell something illegally, especially alcohol or recordings.
examples: Some sites still *bootleg* movies while they are in theaters.
During Prohibition they *bootlegged* whiskey across the state line.
The album was *bootlegged* from a concert tape.
contrast: The g doubles: *bootleg → bootlegged, bootlegging*.

ru: развивать своими силами, поднимать без внешних вложений
gloss: To start or build something using only your own limited resources.
examples: They plan to *bootstrap* the company for one more year.
She *bootstrapped* the business with her own savings.
The team has *bootstrapped* everything out of a spare bedroom.
contrast: The p doubles: *bootstrap → bootstrapped, bootstrapping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*Canada borders the United States*), intransitive (*his tone bordered on rude*)
gloss: To lie along the edge of something, or to be next to it.
examples: Four states *border* Nevada.
Tall hedges *bordered* the driveway.
His confidence is *bordering* on arrogance.
contrast: In the figurative sense it takes **on**: *bordering on absurd*.

gloss: To put a liquid into bottles.
examples: They *bottle* the spring water right at the source.
The winery *bottled* six thousand cases last year.
All of the juice sold here is *bottled* on site.

gloss: To weave three or more strands of hair, rope or cloth together.
examples: Can you *braid* my hair before school?
She *braided* three ribbons into a cord.
The child sat *braiding* blades of grass.

gloss: To force someone to accept ideas by repeating them relentlessly.
examples: Advertising does not *brainwash* anyone overnight.
The group *brainwashed* its recruits over several years.
He claims he was *brainwashed* into signing the papers.

gloss: To divide into two or more parts that go in different directions.
examples: The trail *branches* just past the bridge.
The river *branched* into three narrow channels.
A wide crack was *branching* across the ceiling.

gloss: To wave something, especially a weapon, in a threatening or showy way.
examples: Nobody should *brandish* a weapon in a crowded store.
He *brandished* the letter as proof.
The suspect was *brandishing* a knife when officers arrived.

ru: смело встречать, не бояться; бросать вызов (стихии)
gloss: To face something dangerous or unpleasant instead of avoiding it.
examples: Thousands *brave* the cold for the parade every year.
She *braved* rush-hour traffic to get here on time.
They are *braving* a storm to reach the island.

gloss: To coat food in breadcrumbs before cooking it.
examples: *Bread* the cutlets before you put them in the pan.
He *breaded* the fish with crushed crackers.
The chicken here is *breaded* and baked, not fried.
contrast: The verb *bread* is BRED, exactly like *bred*, the past of *breed*.

gloss: To connect two things or to close the gap between them.
examples: The program is meant to *bridge* the gap between school and work.
A single plank *bridged* the ditch.
Nothing has *bridged* the distance between the two sides.

gloss: To be so full that the contents are about to spill over.
examples: His eyes *brim* with tears whenever he tells that story.
The creek *brimmed* over its banks after the rain.
She came back from the trip *brimming* with ideas.
contrast: The m doubles: *brim → brimmed, brimming*. It normally takes **with**.

gloss: To react with sudden visible anger, or to stand up stiffly like short hairs.
examples: Some readers *bristle* at any criticism of the author.
He *bristled* when I mentioned the deadline.
The roof was *bristling* with antennas.
contrast: The t is silent: BRIS-uhl. In the angry sense it takes **at**.

gloss: To arrange an agreement between two sides who will not deal with each other directly.
examples: Diplomats are still trying to *broker* a ceasefire.
She *brokered* the sale of the entire building.
The deal was *brokered* late on a Friday night.

ru: мрачно размышлять, хандрить; сидеть на яйцах
gloss: To think about something unpleasant for a long time in a gloomy way.
examples: Try not to *brood* over things you cannot change.
He *brooded* about the argument for a week.
She sat *brooding* by the window all afternoon.
contrast: Takes **over** or **about**: *brooding over a mistake*.

gloss: To treat someone with extreme cruelty, or to make someone cruel.
examples: War *brutalizes* everyone it touches.
Guards *brutalized* prisoners for years before anyone noticed.
Several detainees said they had been *brutalized* in custody.
contrast: American English spells it *brutalize*; British English writes *brutalise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*buck the trend*), intransitive (*the horse bucked*)
gloss: To resist something, or, of a horse, to jump with the back arched.
examples: Few companies dare to *buck* the trend right now.
The horse *bucked* and threw him into the dirt.
Their sales have been *bucking* the downturn all year.

ru: сдвигаться с места, сдвинуть; уступать, уступить
transitivity: both — transitive (*I could not budge the lid*), intransitive (*he would not budge*)
gloss: To move slightly, or to change your position in an argument.
examples: The window will not *budge*.
Neither side *budged* an inch during the talks.
The seller has not *budged* on the price.
contrast: Almost always used with a negative: *it won't budge*.

gloss: To swell out beyond the usual surface or shape.
examples: His pockets *bulge* with candy every Halloween.
Her eyes *bulged* when she saw the bill.
The suitcase was *bulging* at the seams.

gloss: To knock down or clear something with heavy machinery, or to force something through.
examples: The city plans to *bulldoze* the old stadium.
Developers *bulldozed* the orchard in a single weekend.
The bill was *bulldozed* through the legislature in two days.

gloss: To do something badly and spoil it through carelessness.
examples: A nervous witness can *bungle* even a simple answer.
The department *bungled* the investigation from the start.
The rollout was so badly *bungled* that they started over.

gloss: To keep something afloat, or to lift someone's spirits or prospects.
examples: Good jobs numbers usually *buoy* the market.
Strong exports *buoyed* the economy last quarter.
The team was *buoyed* by the crowd behind them.
contrast: In American English *buoy* has two syllables, BOO-ee, not BOY.

gloss: To load someone with something heavy or difficult to carry.
examples: I do not want to *burden* you with my problems.
The new rules *burdened* small shops with extra paperwork.
Graduates are *burdened* with enormous debt.
contrast: Takes **with**: *burdened with responsibility*.

gloss: To grow or develop quickly.
examples: Interest in the sport continues to *burgeon*.
The population *burgeoned* after the plant opened.
A *burgeoning* middle class is reshaping the market.

gloss: To polish a surface until it shines, or to improve a reputation.
examples: The trip was meant to *burnish* his image abroad.
She *burnished* the copper pot until it gleamed.
He has spent a decade *burnishing* his credentials.

gloss: To carry a group of people somewhere by bus.
examples: The district *buses* children across town every morning.
They *bused* the fans to the stadium in shifts.
Students were *bused* in from three counties.
contrast: American English keeps one s: *buses, bused, busing*. The doubled forms *busses, bussed, bussing* are British.

gloss: To move around quickly and busily.
examples: Vendors *bustle* through the market every Saturday.
She *bustled* around the kitchen making coffee.
The station was *bustling* with commuters.
contrast: The t is silent: BUS-uhl.

gloss: To go around something instead of through it, or to skip a required step.
examples: You can *bypass* the form and call the office directly.
The new highway *bypassed* the old town center.
By *bypassing* the spam filter, the message reached everyone.

ru: сажать в клетку, посадить в клетку; запирать
gloss: To shut an animal or a person in a cage.
examples: Good zoos no longer *cage* large animals the way they once did.
They *caged* the parrot for the drive home.
He felt *caged* in that windowless office.

gloss: To persuade someone gently and flatteringly to do something.
examples: You cannot *cajole* him into changing his mind.
She *cajoled* her brother into driving her to the airport.
After an hour of *cajoling*, they finally agreed.
contrast: Takes **into**: *cajoled into signing*.

gloss: To adjust an instrument or a judgment so that it measures correctly.
examples: Technicians *calibrate* the scales every morning.
We *calibrated* our expectations after the first week.
The sensor has not been *calibrated* since it was installed.

ru: разбирать на запчасти; поглощать собственные продажи
gloss: To take parts from one thing to repair another, or to take business away from your own product.
examples: A cheaper model could *cannibalize* sales of the flagship.
They *cannibalized* two dead machines to build one that worked.
The new store is *cannibalizing* its own customers.

transitivity: both — intransitive (*the boat capsized*), transitive (*a wave capsized the kayak*)
gloss: To turn over in the water.
examples: Small boats *capsize* easily in that channel.
The ferry *capsized* in heavy seas.
Two kayaks had *capsized* before the guides noticed.

gloss: To feel that something or someone matters to you.
examples: Who *cares* what time it starts?
Honestly, I do not *care* who wins.
She *cared* deeply about her students, even after she retired.
contrast: The standard American idiom is *couldn't care less*, not *could care less*.

gloss: To move fast and out of control, swerving from side to side.
examples: Shopping carts *careen* down that hill all summer.
The truck *careened* into a ditch.
The car went *careening* across three lanes of traffic.
contrast: In American English *careen* is the usual verb for lurching out of control; *career* in that sense is British.

gloss: To describe or draw someone in an exaggerated way that makes them ridiculous.
examples: Critics *caricature* the proposal as a giveaway to the rich.
The cartoon *caricatured* the mayor as a sleeping cat.
His accent has been *caricatured* on television for years.

ru: угонять машину с применением силы, отбирать автомобиль у водителя
gloss: To steal a car by force from the person driving it.
examples: Thieves *carjack* drivers at red lights in that part of the city.
Two men *carjacked* a delivery van downtown.
She was *carjacked* outside her own garage.

gloss: To criticize someone severely, usually in public.
examples: Editorials *castigate* the mayor almost every week.
The judge *castigated* both attorneys for wasting the court's time.
He has been publicly *castigated* for the remark.

gloss: To remove the testicles of a male animal, or to take the force out of something.
examples: Veterinarians routinely *castrate* male cats and dogs.
Amendments *castrated* the bill before the final vote.
The bull had been *castrated* as a calf.

gloss: To cause or speed up a reaction or a change.
examples: Enzymes *catalyze* these reactions at body temperature.
The report *catalyzed* a national debate about policing.
Cheap credit has *catalyzed* a building boom.
contrast: American English spells it *catalyze*; British English writes *catalyse*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the crash catapulted him forward*), intransitive (*he catapulted out of his chair*)
gloss: To throw or be thrown suddenly and violently into a new place or position.
examples: One hit song can *catapult* a singer to fame.
The collision *catapulted* him through the windshield.
That role has *catapulted* her into the spotlight.

gloss: To seal a joint or seam with a waterproof filler.
examples: You should *caulk* around the tub before you paint.
He *caulked* every window frame before winter.
The seams have been *caulked* and sanded smooth.
contrast: The l is silent: *caulk* is KAWK.

gloss: To make something happen, usually something bad.
examples: Heavy rain can *cause* flash flooding in these canyons.
The delay *caused* us to miss our connection.
Storms have *caused* millions of dollars in damage this year.

gloss: To stop resisting and give in to pressure.
examples: Management always *caves* when a strike is threatened.
He *caved* after an hour of arguing.
The company has *caved* to public pressure and issued refunds.
contrast: It takes **to**: *caved to pressure*. With *in* the meaning shifts to collapsing: *the roof caved in*.

gloss: To give up power, land or a right, usually because you have to.
examples: No government wants to *cede* control of its own borders.
Spain *ceded* the islands in 1898.
He has *ceded* the lead to his closest rival.
contrast: *cede* sounds exactly like *seed*.
